approachQuestion.prompt:
Signal tree audit. A read-only perfect binary tree stores one signed integer at every node. A perfect tree has all leaves at the same depth and every non-leaf has exactly two children. Return the sum of all node values. There are n=2^(h+1)-1 nodes for some height 0 <= h <= 17, measured in edges. Child references and values are directly accessible; there are no parent references or cached totals. You may not modify pointers or values. Every intermediate sum fits signed 64-bit. Minimize worst-case total time, then asymptotic peak auxiliary storage. The output is one integer; input nodes are excluded.

Example 1: Input: root value 5, with two leaf children valued -2 and 8. Output: 11.
Example 2: Input: one node valued -4. Output: -4.

options.text: Recursively compute the left subtree total, then the right subtree total, and return those totals plus the current value; retain only a fixed amount per active call.
options.feedback: Every node contributes once. Calls for completed subtrees return before later work, so only the active ancestor chain needs call frames.

options.text: Use an explicit depth-first stack of node references; pop a node, add its value, and push its children if present.
options.feedback: This also visits each node once. In a perfect tree, the pending siblings along a depth-first path occupy the same asymptotic peak storage as recursive calls.

options.text: Traverse using a queue level by level, adding every visited value.
options.feedback: The sum is correct and visits remain efficient, but the bottom levels of a perfect tree keep many pending nodes. A depth-first traversal avoids retaining a whole level.

options.text: Multiply the root value by n and return it.
options.feedback: Node values need not match. A root valued 5 with leaves -2 and 8 sums to 11, whereas this returns 15.

feedback.reason: Peak active call depth differs from the number of calls made over the whole traversal.
details: At a leaf, return its value. Otherwise recursively finish the left subtree, retain its returned scalar total, recursively finish the right subtree, and return the two totals plus the current value. Each frame keeps only a fixed number of references, scalars, and control fields; do not copy subtrees or retain their completed frames.

While the right subtree runs, its parent retains only the left subtree's scalar total. Finished descendants are released rather than accumulated. A perfect tree has logarithmic height; an unrestricted chain-shaped tree would have linear height and would invalidate this stack bound.

“Recursively compute the left subtree total, then the right subtree total, and return those totals plus the current value; retain only a fixed amount per active call.”: Every node contributes once. Calls for completed subtrees return before later work, so only the active ancestor chain needs call frames.

“Use an explicit depth-first stack of node references; pop a node, add its value, and push its children if present.”: This also visits each node once. In a perfect tree, the pending siblings along a depth-first path occupy the same asymptotic peak storage as recursive calls.

“Traverse using a queue level by level, adding every visited value.”: The sum is correct and visits remain efficient, but the bottom levels of a perfect tree keep many pending nodes. A depth-first traversal avoids retaining a whole level.
“Multiply the root value by n and return it.”: Node values need not match. A root valued 5 with leaves -2 and 8 sums to 11, whereas this returns 15.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze recursive-tree-total, not the explicit-stack alternative. What are worst-case time and peak auxiliary space in terms of n for a perfect binary tree? Count the recursion stack and the left total retained while processing the right subtree. Each arithmetic operation and call setup costs constant time. No hashing is used.
constraints: Choose the tightest standard bound for the complete execution. Count peak simultaneously live auxiliary storage; exclude supplied input and required output.
Word arithmetic, indexing, and copying one fixed-size element take constant time. No hashing or recursion is used.

feedback.reason: Visit n nodes, but keep only the logarithmic-height live ancestor chain.
details: Each of n nodes is processed once, so total work is O(n). The maximum live ancestor chain has h+1=log2(n+1) frames. Each retains only constant state, including the completed left total, so auxiliary storage is O(log(n+1)). Completed calls do not accumulate. Input nodes are neither copied nor counted as auxiliary; the output is scalar.
“O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: This counts all frames ever created as simultaneously live. Returned subtree calls have already been released.
“O(log(n + 1)) time, O(log(n + 1)) auxiliary space”: Only the active depth is logarithmic; both subtrees are explored and all n values contribute.
“O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The recursive method has a growing stack even though it allocates no separate container.
